accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are accurate: discovery is separate from HTTP; delegation and address/alias types are scoped; ordinary TTL and negative caches differ; failures are not absence; steering cannot migrate connections; DNSSEC is separate from HTTPS identity. RFC updates and TLS followup checked live.

evidence.quote: A new TTL cannot rewrite an old cached answer

mechanisms.reason: The reader can trace stub/recursive referrals and alias target resolution, calculate cache lifetime, plan overlap, distinguish negative and failure answers, and locate discovery versus application failures. Failover needs separate detection, answer change and reachable spare capacity.

evidence.quote: A referral points the resolver toward them; it is not the final host address.

coherence.reason: Every card objective and prerequisite is taught in sequence: names, actors, records, cache aging, absent/failure results, steering, diagnosis and trust. Diagrams at indexes 1 and 3 correctly identify teaching hierarchy/referrals and independent old-cache/new-authority timelines.

evidence.quote: Locate the failed step before changing DNS or the application.

decisions.reason: Actionable choices include early TTL lowering with observed overlap, refresh-cost tradeoff, diagnosis by name/type/status, capacity-aware failover and retaining HTTPS checks after DNSSEC. No global propagation deadline or exact HTTP split is promised.

evidence.quote: Returning east for half of lookups does not guarantee half of HTTP requests reach east.

clarity.reason: DNS actors, zones, delegation, cache, address families, TTL and negative-result terms are defined at first use. Reserved teaching names avoid deployment claims; concrete timelines explain transfer. Shared renderer/CSS already reviewed; diagram labels and captions match prose.

evidence.quote: Distinguish an answer about absence from a failure to obtain an answer.

outcomes.reason: All eight criteria satisfied: learner traces stub/recursive/referral/authority roles, zone/delegation, alias-to-A/AAAA target and address family, cache shortcuts and separate alias state, then HTTPS hostname/path without treating DNS as HTTP or health proof.

All three criteria satisfied: learner calculates 12:59 old expiry, rejects 12:01 purge assumption, lowers TTL before prior lifetime ages out, maintains overlap and monitors connections, explains extra queries/dependency and no universal cutoff.
All three criteria satisfied: learner uses negative answer own lifetime independent of positive TTL, distinguishes name absence from missing AAAA and SERVFAIL, and recognizes cached failures.

All four criteria satisfied: learner separates health/operator policy from records, explains lookup/request imbalance via shared caches/connections, delayed old-address traffic/no connection migration and reachable healthy replacement headroom.

All four criteria satisfied: learner explains cached/open-session survival, queries client resolver name/type/status/TTL then authority/delegation, separates expected-address connection/HTTPS/HTTP500 investigation and limits redundant DNS under shared misconfiguration.

All three criteria satisfied: learner explains signed chain from trusted key and origin/integrity, rejects query privacy/health guarantees, and retains HTTPS certificate validation for original requested hostname despite alias.

sourceChecks.claim: Cloudflare DNS lookup and HTTP steps explicitly separate address discovery from the later web request; caching and stub descriptions support skipped lookup work. Typed resource model corroborated in RFC1034.
AWS Route53 walkthrough verifies resolver root/TLD/domain visits, authoritative zone answer and cached delegation skipping; RFC1034 referral and resolver sections corroborate the teaching hierarchy.
AWS record type sections verify A IPv4, AAAA IPv6 and CNAME target name. RFC1034 alias algorithm includes CNAME then restarts at target and can return target address in same answer.

RFC8767 explicitly permits stale expired answers during refresh failure; RFC1034 TTL section defines cache lifetime and advance lowering. Independent cache state explains exact timeline and absence of push/global connection cutover.

RFC9520 distinguishes useful absent responses from resolution failure, names NXDOMAIN/NODATA, documents SOA-based negative TTL and requires failure caching. Adding positive data cannot update a disconnected existing cache.

AWS failover page explicitly requires health checks/policy selecting responses, not automatic records. Previously verified cache and connection behavior explains non-exact request split and delayed failover; replacement capacity remains separate.

RFC1034 resolver/referral/error/resource sections support checking queried name/type, authority and cached data separately. AWS DNS walkthrough and RFC9110 already inspected support later HTTP error distinction; replicated wrong state does not correct itself.

RFC4033 verifies origin/integrity, signed trust chain/anchor and absence of confidentiality. RFC9525 reference-identifier rules explicitly prohibit substituting intermediate DNS names for original service identity; HTTPS certificate checks remain required.
